treatments.name: TMS Therapy
treatments.title: TMS Therapy for depression
treatments.summary: When antidepressants have not brought enough relief, TMS offers a different way to treat depression. It uses magnetic stimulation rather than medication and does not require surgery or anesthesia.

seo.title: TMS | Westlake Fictional Practice Concept
seo.description: Learn what TMS is, why it is used for depression, and what treatment involves. A fictional Westlake Psychiatry & Therapy example.

sections.heading: What is TMS?
paragraphs: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a noninvasive treatment that delivers focused magnetic pulses through a coil placed against the scalp. These pulses stimulate brain circuits involved in mood regulation, with the goal of reducing depression symptoms.
TMS is not an antidepressant medication. You remain awake during treatment, without sedation or anesthesia.

sections.heading: Why is TMS used for depression?
paragraphs: Depression can continue to affect your energy, interest in life, and ability to manage everyday tasks even after trying medication. TMS offers another treatment option when antidepressants have not helped enough or have been difficult to tolerate.

Research supports TMS for reducing depression symptoms. The aim is meaningful relief that helps you return to daily life; the degree and timing of improvement vary. TMS can be part of a broader plan that also includes medication or talk therapy.

sections.heading: What does treatment feel like?
paragraphs: You sit in a chair while the coil delivers magnetic pulses. You may hear clicking and feel tapping on your scalp. Before treatment begins, the clinician identifies the treatment area and adjusts the stimulation settings.

A typical course involves appointments five days a week for four to six weeks. Session length and the full schedule depend on the device and treatment plan. This is a general expectation, not a fixed schedule for every patient.

sections.heading: How is progress assessed?
paragraphs: Your clinician reviews changes in symptoms and daily functioning throughout treatment. Improvement may build over a series of sessions. Follow-up care depends on your response and whether symptoms return.

sections.heading: Safety and suitability
paragraphs: Headache and scalp discomfort can occur; seizures are a rare risk. Tell your clinician about any seizure history, implanted devices, or metal in or near your head. Some implants or metal can make TMS unsuitable.
An evaluation considers your depression, previous treatments, and medical history before deciding whether TMS is appropriate.

treatments.name: Spravato
treatments.title: Spravato for treatment-resistant depression
treatments.summary: Spravato is an FDA-approved esketamine nasal spray for adults with treatment-resistant depression. It offers another treatment option when antidepressants have not provided enough relief.

seo.title: Spravato | Westlake Fictional Practice Concept
seo.description: Learn what Spravato is, why it is used for treatment-resistant depression, and what supervised treatment involves. A fictional practice example.

sections.heading: What is Spravato?
paragraphs: Spravato contains esketamine, a medicine related to ketamine. It is given as a nasal spray under medical supervision, rather than taken at home. It acts on NMDA receptors involved in glutamate signaling in the brain; its exact antidepressant mechanism is not fully understood.

sections.heading: Why is it used for depression?
paragraphs: Trying treatment and still feeling depressed can be discouraging. Treatment-resistant depression generally means that at least two antidepressant treatments have not provided enough improvement. Spravato offers a different medication approach for adults in this situation.

For treatment-resistant depression, Spravato can be prescribed on its own or with an oral antidepressant. The goal is relief from symptoms that interfere with daily life. Response varies, so continued treatment depends on how you are doing.

sections.heading: What happens during a visit?
paragraphs: You use the nasal spray under supervision, then stay for monitoring for at least two hours. The care team checks your blood pressure and breathing and determines when you can safely leave.
Arrange a ride home. Do not drive or operate machinery until the next day after a restful sleep.

sections.heading: How often is treatment given?
paragraphs: For treatment-resistant depression, treatment usually starts twice weekly for four weeks. Visits then become less frequent, depending on response. Your clinician assesses benefit after the initial phase and adjusts the ongoing schedule.

sections.heading: Important safety information
paragraphs: Spravato can cause sleepiness, dizziness, nausea, and dissociation—a feeling of disconnection from yourself or your surroundings. Risks also include increased blood pressure, breathing problems, and abuse or misuse. It carries an antidepressant warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviors, especially in younger patients.

Spravato is available only through a restricted safety program called REMS. Review the Medication Guide and your medical history with your clinician. It does not replace emergency care or hospitalization when needed.

providers.name: Dr. Elena Morgan
providers.tagline: Adult psychiatric care with a focus on depression and finding a path forward when previous treatment has not helped enough.
bioParagraphs: Dr. Elena Morgan helps adults navigate depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and ADHD, including those who have tried treatment and still feel stuck.

Her fellowship training in interventional psychiatry informs her work with TMS and Spravato. She considers your symptoms, previous treatments, medical history, and goals when exploring options. Medication visits include time to talk about what you are experiencing and how care fits into your everyday life.
Dr. Morgan and Jordan provide psychiatric care and medication management. Rachel provides regular talk therapy. When you choose both, the clinicians work together across separate appointments.

providers.name: Jordan Lee
providers.tagline: Adult psychiatric care informed by a background in psychology and primary care, with a focus on clear medication guidance.
bioParagraphs: Jordan Lee brings a background in psychology and primary care to adult psychiatric evaluations and medication management. That experience informs a practical approach to understanding how mood, attention, sleep, and physical health affect everyday life.

Jordan works with Dr. Morgan to explore treatment options, explain medication benefits and side effects, and review how your care is progressing. Visits make room for your questions and preferences, whether you are starting treatment or reconsidering an existing plan.
Jordan’s Psychiatry CAQ recognizes additional knowledge and experience in psychiatric care beyond general physician assistant certification.

providers.name: Rachel Ellis
providers.tagline: Trauma-informed therapy for adults navigating anxiety, relationship difficulties, and the effects of trauma or racialized stress.
bioParagraphs: Rachel Ellis is a licensed clinical social worker with a doctorate in social work and 17 years of experience supporting individuals and families. At Westlake, she provides individual therapy for adults navigating trauma, racialized stress, depression, anxiety, and relationship difficulties.

Rachel considers the whole person: your identity, family relationships, community, and the wider pressures affecting your life. Her approach makes space for the impact of racism and cultural experiences without asking you to set those parts of your story aside.

Through trauma-informed therapy, Rachel helps you explore patterns that cause pain, strengthen your sense of connection, and work toward changes that matter to you. She offers regular talk therapy on its own or alongside psychiatric care with Dr. Morgan or Jordan.

insurance.headline: Insurance Coverage
insurance.summary: We accept insurance for psychiatric care and talk therapy. Contact the office before scheduling to confirm participation for your provider and plan.

verification.description: Insurance participation varies by provider, plan, and service. For TMS and Spravato, ask about coverage requirements, prior authorization, and your share of the cost.

insurance.disclaimer: Your insurance plan determines coverage and benefits. Listing a carrier does not guarantee coverage for a specific service.

faqs.question: Do I need medication, therapy, or both?
faqs.answer: You do not have to decide before asking for care. Psychiatric care explores symptoms and treatment options, including medication. Talk therapy offers regular time to work through feelings and patterns. You can use either service or both.

faqs.question: Would I see the same person for medication and therapy?
faqs.answer: Our psychiatrist and physician assistant provide psychiatric care. Our therapist provides ongoing talk therapy. If you choose both, you have separate appointments with the relevant clinicians.

faqs.question: What happens at my first appointment?
faqs.answer: For psychiatric care, your first visit is an evaluation of your concerns, health history, previous treatments, and goals. For therapy, your first session explores what brings you in and what you want help with.

faqs.question: When might I explore TMS or Spravato?
faqs.answer: If depression continues despite previous antidepressant treatment, an evaluation can help you explore additional options. Your symptoms alone do not establish eligibility for either treatment.

faqs.question: Does accepting insurance mean my treatment is covered?
faqs.answer: No. Participation and benefits depend on your provider, plan, and service. TMS and Spravato may require prior authorization. Ask about coverage and out-of-pocket costs before starting care.
